title: Raising chickens for eggs
text: Laying hens need a balanced commercial diet, daily access to clean water, and, as needed, supplemental calcium such as crushed oyster shell. Grit supports digestion, while dust-bathing material helps with feather and mite management. Nest boxes and elevated roosting areas support normal behavior. A hen may begin laying around six months of age, with peak production often in the first two years. Egg production commonly changes with age, breed, season, and daylight, and eggs should be collected twice daily. Clean coops and feeding equipment regularly.

title: Housing Backyard Chickens
text: A backyard coop should protect birds from weather and predators, provide feed and water access, and allow enough floor area for comfortable movement. Practical minimums include ventilation that keeps fresh air moving while avoiding direct winter drafts. In summer, ventilation removes warm, stale air; in cold weather, controlled air exchange limits moisture and harmful gases. Nesting areas should be accessible and kept clean. Regular inspection of openings, perches, and bedding helps prevent injuries and escape.

title: Enclosing the Backyard Flock
text: A fully enclosed flock needs all routine care inside the structure: feed, water, appropriate light, clean bedding, ventilation, and protection from predators and pests. Ventilation design should account for season, bird count, and the number and placement of openings or fans. Artificial lighting may support consistent production during shorter winter days, but the schedule should suit the birds and avoid creating unnecessary stress. Keeping the flock enclosed also makes a biosecurity plan easier to maintain.

title: Build a Clean Routine
text: Clean coops and other enclosures reduce the spread of harmful germs. Move the birds to a separate area, remove manure and bedding, clean surfaces, and disinfect with a product used according to its label. Dedicated boots or disposable boot covers and dedicated clothing help prevent movement of pathogens. Change protective gear between groups or houses. Cleaning and disinfection take time and should not be attempted around birds without following label and safety instructions.

title: Biosecurity Basics
text: Biosecurity is a set of daily practices that limits disease entry and spread. Key habits include restricting visitor access, separating poultry from wild birds and other animals, using dedicated tools and footwear, cleaning vehicles and equipment, and controlling the movement of feed and supplies. Quarantine and disease monitoring reduce risk when birds join or return to a flock. A written routine helps the keeper find weak points and respond consistently.

title: How To Spot Sickness
text: Birds may show illness through changes in appetite, energy, breathing, movement, or egg production. Warning signs include respiratory discharge or sneezing, swelling of the head or neck, unusual discoloration, twisting of the head or neck, paralysis, stumbling, and sudden death. Keep observation records and isolate a sick bird only when it can be done safely. Suspected highly contagious disease should be reported quickly to a State veterinarian or USDA APHIS.

title: Backyard Poultry
organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Backyard poultry can carry Salmonella even when they look healthy. Keep birds outdoors rather than inside living areas, wash hands thoroughly after handling birds or equipment, and keep poultry supplies away from kitchens and food preparation areas. Do not kiss or snuggle birds or eat and drink where they live. Young children under five, older adults, pregnant people, and immunocompromised people face higher risk and should have close supervision or limited direct contact.

title: Keep chickens and other poultry out of your home
organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Poultry droppings and dust can spread germs to shoes, clothing, hands, coops, and household surfaces. Store dedicated footwear and cleaning supplies outside living areas, clean equipment outdoors, and wash hands with soap and water after contact. Avoid bringing birds into kitchens or bathrooms and prevent children from handling birds unsupervised. Thorough cooking of eggs and poultry reduces foodborne illness risk.

title: Salmonella and Backyard Poultry
organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Salmonella from backyard poultry can spread through direct contact and contaminated droppings, feed, water, bedding, cages, or soil. It can contaminate hands and then enter the mouth. Common illness symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps. Seek medical care for severe symptoms, dehydration, bloody diarrhea, persistent fever, or symptoms that do not improve. Use handwashing and environmental controls to reduce exposure.

title: Caring for Chickens in Cold Climates
text: Healthy adult chickens usually need protection from wind and wet conditions more than added heat. Dry, draft-free housing with enough ventilation is important because moisture from breath and droppings can condense and cause frostbite or respiratory problems. Keep feed and unfrozen water available, inspect combs and wattles, and clean nest boxes regularly. In cold weather, gather eggs promptly because fresh eggs can freeze and cracked shells create a food-safety concern.

title: Keep Your Chickens Healthy and Producing During Winter Months
organization: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
text: Feathers insulate chickens by trapping a warm air layer, but wind and damp air can reduce that protection. A coop should block wind at bird level while still exchanging moist air; an airtight enclosure can allow condensation and harmful gases to accumulate. Watch for frostbitten combs and wattles, especially where humidity is high. Protect water from freezing and preserve dry bedding and clean, well-drained outdoor areas.

title: Preventing Heat Stress in Chickens
text: Heat stress can occur as temperature and humidity rise beyond a bird's ability to release heat. Watch for panting, excessive drinking, and lethargy. Increase air movement at bird level, provide plentiful cool water and functioning drinkers, offer shade, and use feeders and work routines that reduce additional heat exposure. Clean water lines and drinkers regularly. Ventilation is usually the first control measure; fan and building capacity may still be limiting factors.

title: Establishing a Backyard Poultry Flock
organization: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
text: Young chicks need a draft-free brooder, an appropriate heat source, chick-sized waterers, and starter feed formulated for their age. Temperature and behavior guide adjustments: chicks that crowd together may be cold, while chicks panting or spread away from the heat may be too warm. Reduce brooder temperature gradually as birds develop, and raise drinkers or use shallow options to prevent falls and chilling. Follow manufacturer guidance for safe brooder placement.

title: Avian Influenza and Biosecurity
text: Avian influenza viruses can spread through direct contact, contaminated surfaces, clothing, equipment, vehicles, and wild birds. Keep domestic poultry away from wild waterfowl and areas they use, limit outside visitors and shared equipment, and clean and disinfect supplies. Do not bring birds or equipment from uncertain sources into the flock area. Sudden illness or deaths should trigger isolation and prompt reporting to a State veterinarian or USDA.

title: Poultry Production and Management
text: Poultry housing affects health and performance through air quality, temperature, humidity, and light. Dust and ammonia can irritate birds, while poor ventilation can make respiratory or humidity problems worse. Lighting needs vary by age and production goal, and pullet transition to lay should be planned to support egg production. Regular observation of feed intake, behavior, manure, and egg output can help keepers identify change early.

title: Food Safety for Eggs
organization: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
text: Collect eggs frequently and refrigerate clean, unwashed eggs as appropriate for local handling practices. Discard cracked or dirty eggs according to the advice of local health or food-safety authorities. Wash hands and surfaces after handling raw eggs. Eggs and dishes containing eggs should be cooked safely and left at room temperature only for short periods. People at higher risk of foodborne illness should follow additional precautions.

title: Predator-Proofing a Chicken Coop
text: Common chicken predators include raccoons, rats, owls, hawks, and domestic cats. Keep birds in a secure enclosure at night and close openings that could admit a predator. Repair weak doors and screens, remove unnecessary stored objects near the coop that offer cover, and inspect the area regularly. Store feed in sealed containers so it does not attract rodents or other wildlife. Adequate outdoor supervision during the day adds another layer of protection.

title: Using Litter and Bedding in Poultry Houses
text: Dry bedding helps maintain foot health and limits the buildup of wet manure and odor. Choose bedding that is absorbent and free of dust, mold, and harmful contaminants. Remove caked or heavily soiled material and replenish clean bedding before moisture becomes a persistent problem. Bedding that remains damp should prompt a review of ventilation, roof leaks, waterers, and drainage. Compost manure according to local rules and ensure it is not accessible to poultry or wildlife.

title: Water Quality and Waterers for Poultry
text: Poultry should have continuous access to clean, cool water. Check drinkers daily and clean them often enough to prevent algae, feed, manure, or biofilm buildup. Ensure all birds can reach the water and that the delivery system is at a practical height and flow. Freezing, contamination, or equipment failure can quickly reduce intake. Changes in water consumption can be an early clue to heat stress or health problems.

title: Poultry Nutrition
text: Feeding by a bird's age and purpose helps prevent nutrient deficiencies and excesses. Commercially balanced starter, grower, and layer feeds are designed for major life stages, while table scraps should remain supplements rather than the main diet. Calcium needs rise when hens produce eggs, and inappropriate food or sudden diet changes can reduce intake or cause digestive problems. Water quality and feeder access are just as important as the feed itself.

title: Molting and Egg Production
text: Molting is a normal annual process in which a hen replaces feathers, often accompanied by a temporary decrease or pause in egg production. Adequate balanced nutrition and low stress support feather regrowth and recovery. Sudden or prolonged changes in laying, abnormal eggs, lethargy, or poor appetite can indicate additional issues. Daylight, age, breed, nutrition, and season all influence egg production patterns.

title: Introducing New Chickens
organization: University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources
text: Before birds join a flock, obtain them from a reputable source and review health records or testing when relevant. USDA guidance also recommends separating new or returning birds for at least 30 days from the established flock. Use a separate area with dedicated clothing and tools, observe appetite and breathing, and clean and disinfect equipment. Gradual introduction after quarantine reduces disease risk and gives keepers time to observe aggression and establish compatible spaces.

title: Cleaning and Disinfecting Poultry Equipment
text: Start cleaning with manure and organic debris removed, then wash surfaces and allow them to dry. Disinfectants work best on clean surfaces and must be mixed, used, and stored according to the product label. Protect birds from concentrated solutions and observe required contact time. Waterers and feeders need regular cleaning because feed residue and water films can support microbial growth. Keep a written cleaning schedule and avoid using products not approved for the surface or intended use.

title: Backyard Poultry Zoonotic Disease
text: Poultry can harbor organisms that infect people even when birds appear healthy. Handwashing after bird or coop contact is a central prevention measure, and food, drink, and tobacco should remain outside animal areas. Buy birds from sources that follow recognized health monitoring programs when possible. Keep high-risk household members away from close contact and from handling eggs or cleaning equipment. Report unusual flock illness to the appropriate animal-health authority.
